# Block 2: Choosing the right figure {.unnumbered} ## The chart-type table Before anything else, the structure of your data determines the chart type. Variable count and variable type narrow the choice. The table below is a guide rather than a rule: your scientific question may demand something else, but you should be able to justify it. | Variable 1 | Variable 2 | Variable 3 | Default chart | |---|---|---|---| | Continuous | — | — | Raincloud (`ggdist::stat_halfeye` + boxplot + jittered points) | | Continuous | Continuous | — | Scatter plot | | Continuous | Continuous | Discrete | Scatter plot with colour and shape mapped to the discrete variable | | Discrete | — | — | Bar chart of counts | | Discrete | Continuous | — | Raincloud per group | | Discrete | Discrete | — | Heatmap of counts | | Discrete | Discrete | Continuous | Heatmap of the continuous variable | | Date | Continuous | — | Line chart | | Date | Continuous | Discrete | Line chart, one line per group | A few rules are worth memorising: no pie charts (use a labelled proportion); no 3D effects of any kind; no dual y-axes (use two panels instead); no dynamite plots (bar charts of means with error bars) where raw data are available, so show a raincloud or strip plot instead (Weissgerber et al., 2015). **Chart chooser.** Use the table to pick a default: - Wing length of 40 butterflies from each of three sites: - Daily soil temperature over a year at two field stations: - Number of nests found in each habitat × year combination: ## Descriptive vs explanatory framing Every figure communicates at two levels: it presents the data, and it makes an argument. The framing of the title and the legend determines which level the reader engages with first. A **descriptive title** states what the figure shows in neutral language: *"Body mass of three penguin species in the Palmer Archipelago"*. The reader is shown the data and invited to interpret. An **explanatory title** states what the figure means: *"Gentoo penguins are substantially heavier than Adelie and Chinstrap"*. The reader is told the conclusion and invited to verify it from the data. Neither is wrong. The choice is determined by the audience. Journal figures and lab reports use descriptive framing because the reader is expected to bring their own judgement and the figure legend below carries the necessary methodological detail. Talks, posters, and public engagement use explanatory framing because the reader has limited time, attention, or technical background to derive the conclusion themselves. ## Audience design The same finding becomes a different figure for different audiences. The table below summarises the design choices that should change with context: | Element | Journal / lab report | Poster | Talk | Public engagement | |---|---|---|---|---| | Title above figure | No | Yes (explanatory) | Yes (explanatory) | Yes (explanatory) | | Figure legend below | Yes (four elements) | Optional, abbreviated | No | No | | Direct labelling | Where it does not break convention | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Highlighting (grey out non-focal groups) | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Reference lines and annotations | Sparingly | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Statistical detail | Precise p-values where shown | Abbreviated | One key result | None or one sentence | | Base font size | 12pt (floor) | 16–20pt | 14–18pt | 14–18pt | | Raw data shown | Always where n permits | Always | Always | Where it clarifies | | Interactivity (hover, zoom) | Supplementary only | No | No | Yes, on the web | Every figure must stay honest and accessible whatever the audience. What changes are the design choices needed to communicate with that audience. ## Interactive figures On a web page, a lab website, or a Quarto HTML report, the reader can *interact* with a figure. `ggiraph` turns a `ggplot` into an interactive one with almost no new code: swap `geom_point()` for `geom_point_interactive()`, add a `tooltip` (what appears on hover) and a `data_id` (what gets highlighted together), and wrap the plot in `girafe()`. Hover over a penguin below: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggiraph) p <- penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species, tooltip = paste0(species, " (", sex, ")\n", body_mass_g, " g, ", island), data_id = species)) + geom_point_interactive(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = "Species") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) girafe(ggobj = p, options = list(opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.15;"))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Because `data_id = species`, hovering on one penguin highlights its whole species and fades the rest: the *highlighting* row of the audience table, under the reader's control. Interactivity is a bonus, never a requirement. A figure must still work as a static image, because PDFs, printouts and most journal pages cannot hover. ### Exercise 2: Same data, four audiences :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Same data, four audiences :::: ::::{.task-container} You have one finding: > **Gentoo penguins are substantially heavier than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins** 🏆 **Guess the audience (solo, 12 minutes).** Draw your secret audience by running `sample(1:4, 1)`, and don't tell anyone which number you got: 1. Journal figure (specialist reader, no time pressure) 2. Conference poster (3 seconds to attract, 2 minutes to engage) 3. Seminar slide (audience cannot control viewing time) 4. Museum infographic (non-specialist, no assumed technical knowledge) Build the best figure of the finding for *your* audience from `penguins_complete`, using the audience table above. Don't put the audience in the title! Post a screenshot in the chat. The facilitator shows each figure on screen in turn and everyone posts their guess (1–4). You score a point for every correct guess about your figure. If nobody can place your figure, it was not designed for any particular audience. (Small group? Build two figures for two different audiences, so there are enough to guess.) **Bonus:** if you got the museum, make it interactive with `ggiraph`. What would a visitor want to see when they hover? :::: :::
